title: Rapid mixing of Gibbs samplers via quantum Dobrushin--Shlosman conditions
abstract: Classical Dobrushin--Shlosman theory uses heat-bath block updates to identify sharp temperature thresholds for establishing the rapid mixing of Gibbs samplers. In particular, these mixing guarantees often hold even when stricter single-site conditions fail. We extend this approach to noncommuting quantum lattice systems through a quantum Dobrushin--Shlosman condition for finite-block dynamics, which we call smoothed heat-bath dynamics. We establish this condition in two regimes. For finite-range quantum spin chains at every fixed finite temperature, we prove logarithmic trace-norm mixing in system size, with normalized bounds uniform in on-site fields and single exponential in inverse temperature. We also prove stability under small local perturbations of interacting, possibly noncommuting reference Hamiltonians on graphs of polynomial volume growth. For classical references with bounded local interactions, uniform strong spatial mixing implies our quantum condition. With bounded local terms and fixed physical, geometric and block parameters, the resulting samplers prepare Gibbs states to trace-norm error $\varepsilon$ using $N\operatorname{polylog}(N/\varepsilon)$ gates and classical operations.   Our block updates combine a local Gibbs reset with quantum belief propagation to incorporate interactions across the block boundary, yielding exactly Gibbs-preserving, KMS-reversible channels. Two independently tunable parameters control contraction: an internal evolution time suppresses the influence of sites inside a block, while the block size allows interior contraction to dominate boundary influence. This finite-time relaxation has no counterpart in a classical heat-bath block update.
summary: This paper extends classical mixing theory to quantum lattice systems by defining a 'quantum Dobrushin–Shlosman condition' for finite-block dynamics. It proves that quantum Gibbs samplers can rapidly mix to the true thermal state using controlled block updates. This has significant implications for designing efficient quantum algorithms to simulate thermal equilibrium in quantum matter.
main_problem: The paper aims to extend classical Dobrushin–Shlosman theory to establish rapid mixing guarantees for Gibbs samplers in noncommuting quantum lattice systems.
main_result: Logarithmic trace-norm mixing is proven for quantum spin chains at fixed finite temperatures, and the quantum Dobrushin–Shlosman condition is shown to be stable under small local perturbations.
method: The authors construct 'smoothed heat-bath dynamics' using a combination of local Gibbs resets and quantum belief propagation to define block updates that preserve the Gibbs state.
model_or_system: The focus is on quantum lattice systems, such as quantum spin chains, governed by finite-range Hamiltonians. The target state is the Gibbs state $\sigma_{ eta,H} = e^{- eta H} / 	ext{Tr}(e^{- eta H})$.
key_observables: Trace-norm error ($\varepsilon$), covariance of observables ($	ext{Cov}_{\sigma_ eta}(A, B)$), and the contraction constant $\kappa$ derived from the quantum Dobrushin–Shlosman condition.
important_parameters: Inverse temperature ($ eta$), block size ($\ell$), evolution time ($T$), and perturbation strength ($\delta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the existence of positive-exponent Gibbs operators and the ability to decompose the system into localized neighborhoods (cuts) for bounding correlations.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the construction of single-site and block updates, detailing the algebraic steps from Gibbs replacement to the final KMS-reversible channel $\Phi_{B_x}(T)$.
paper_structure: The paper builds by first establishing bounds on correlations using inclusion-exclusion principles for multiple cuts, then constructing the block update via quantum belief propagation, and finally proving the mixing bounds and stability under perturbations.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous, quantifiable methods to simulate thermalization processes in quantum many-body systems, which is crucial for understanding quantum thermalization and quantum simulation algorithms.
